blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — recognize worsening disease trends and use prescribed risk-reduction instructions
stem: A client with asthma has a written action plan that includes peak expiratory flow zones. Which statement shows correct understanding of home peak-flow monitoring?

options.A: I will compare each reading with the predicted value for people my age and size, then use that percentage to decide which action-plan zone applies.
options.B: I will compare each reading with my established personal best and use the zone together with my symptoms to follow the written action-plan instructions.
options.C: I will use the highest reading from that day as my new baseline so the action-plan zones adjust to how my breathing is changing over time.
options.D: If my symptoms worsen while the peak-flow reading is still in my usual zone, I will wait for the number to fall before following symptom-based action-plan steps.

rationale: CDC asthma action-plan guidance is individualized. Its green, yellow, and red zones describe both symptoms and peak-flow measurements relative to the client's own best peak flow. Therefore B is correct: the client compares readings with an established personal best and follows the written plan using both the zone and clinical symptoms. A is incorrect because the CDC action plan uses the person's best peak flow rather than a population-predicted value to define the zones. C is incorrect because the action-plan baseline is the established personal best, not a new daily maximum that is repeatedly reset. D is incorrect because the CDC zones include symptom criteria as well as peak-flow criteria, so worsening symptoms can trigger the plan even when the number has not yet crossed a lower peak-flow threshold.
educational_objective: Teach clients using a peak-flow-based asthma action plan to compare readings with their established personal best and to follow the written green/yellow/red-zone instructions using both peak-flow changes and symptoms.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Living with Asthma — Asthma Action Plans
source_locator: Asthma Action Plans — Green Zone, Yellow Zone, and Red Zone sections: each zone lists symptom criteria and peak-flow criteria expressed relative to the individual's best peak flow; the page directs clients to work with a health care provider to create and follow their own asthma action plan.
source_claim_supported: Home peak-flow action-plan zones are individualized to the client's personal best and are interpreted together with symptoms and the written medication/action instructions.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential, printed p.13/PDF p.17: recognize trends and changes in client condition and intervene as needed; monitor results of diagnostic testing and intervene as needed; educate clients on methods to prevent complications associated with diagnosed illness/disease.
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four alternatives to remove the distractor-only absolute term, replace implausible statements with realistic home-monitoring errors, and make the educational objective specific to personal-best peak flow plus symptom-based action-plan use.

audit_findings.stem: PASS — specifies an existing written action plan with peak-flow zones and asks only for correct home-monitoring understanding.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS as distractor — population-predicted values are plausible in pulmonary testing, but CDC action-plan zones are based on the individual's best peak flow.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS — directly matches CDC's individualized peak-flow zones and its use of both symptoms and peak-flow criteria.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — daily readings are monitored, but redefining the baseline from each day's highest value would defeat the fixed personal-best comparison used by the action plan.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — plausible overreliance on the meter, but CDC zones explicitly include symptom criteria that can trigger action independent of the numeric peak-flow criterion.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — only B preserves both required concepts: personal-best comparison and use of symptom plus peak-flow criteria within the written plan.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — A uses the wrong reference, C changes the reference baseline, and D incorrectly postpones symptom-based action.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — alternatives are similar in length and clinical specificity; no distractor-only 'only/always/never' wording remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — trend recognition, diagnostic monitoring, and prevention of complications from a diagnosed illness align directly with Reduction of Risk Potential.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether peak-flow readings alone could define the zone and whether a predicted reference could substitute for personal best. Current CDC guidance repeatedly expresses peak-flow thresholds as a percentage of the person's best and also lists symptom criteria in each zone. B remains uniquely correct.
